newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kinkel wants more dialogue with Iran after poll.
newsitem.headline: Kinkel wants more dialogue with Iran after poll.

text.p: German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said on Thursday the West should strive for more dialogue with Iran after last month's election of moderate Shi'ite Moslem cleric Mohammad Khatami as president.
Kinkel's remarks suggested Bonn was keen to mend ties damaged by a recent Berlin court verdict that Iran's leaders ordered terrorist attacks on Iranian exiles.

His words coincided with an interview with U.S. President Bill Clinton in a German newspaper that suggested Washington might be ready to soften its stance against Tehran, which it has long reviled as an alleged sponsor of international terrorism.

"Politically we must make sure that the clash of cultures does not turn into a conflict. That is why I believe more dialogue with Islam is so important," Kinkel said in a speech in Bonn to mark 50 years since the launch of the Marshall Plan for the post-war reconstruction of Europe.

"The dialogue should be about a civil society based on freedom and responsibility. It would be a good thing if Iran were to stop excluding itself from this," he said, according to a text of his speech released ahead of the evening event.
"The election of Iranian President Mohammad Khatami makes us somewhat hopeful that this will come about," Kinkel said.

Clinton, who met German Chancellor Helmut Kohl in Washington on Wednesday, told the Bild mass-circulation daily that the United States and Germany should seek a more common approach to countries such as Iran.

"In respect of criminal states such as Iran, we must work harder to ensure that our differences do not overshadow our much greater agreement on ways to contain terrorism and the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction," Clinton was quoted as saying, in German translation.
Khatami's election has been seen by some U.S. political analysts as adding to the pressure on Clinton from his European allies to rethink the long U.S. drive to isolate Iran as a "rogue nation".

Germany and other European countries are seen using the Iranian election results to patch up ties with Iran, damaged after the Berlin court concluded in April that Iranian leaders had ordered the 1992 killing of four Iranian Kurds in Berlin.

Before the verdict, Germany had been the main champion of the European Union's policy of "critical dialogue" with Iran, despite the U.S. policy of isolating the country, and Kinkel had been its chief proponent.
